Sam Altman on the one AI policy where OpenAI and Anthropic still disagree:

Brendan Bordelon asked Altman to name a specific policy that Anthropic supports and OpenAI doesn't, at either the federal or state level.

First, he pointed out how much the two companies now agree on:

"You guys are now on the same page when it comes to pacing the frontier of China. Same page with third party evaluators. What's just one differentiator?"

Altman says the difference is which models should face oversight at all:

"The last I heard, one of the differentiators is we don't want any restrictions or testing on anything but the frontier models. We do not want to slow down people that make very powerful, but not the absolute frontier."

Both companies support testing and third-party evaluation. Where they split is scope.

In Altman's framing, OpenAI wants restrictions and testing applied only to frontier models, with nothing below them. That leaves out models he himself calls "very powerful."

He explains the reasoning:

"In the spirit of really focusing on the potential catastrophic risks…"

Then he names the cost directly:

"…even though I believe that if you don't put any testing or any oversight on models that are one or two generations behind the frontier, I accept that bad things will happen with those. I would not go advocate a licensing regime for those."

So OpenAI's position, as @sama states it, has three parts:

Oversight should concentrate on the potential catastrophic risks at the absolute frontier.

Models one or two generations behind should face no testing or oversight requirements.

That will lead to some harm, and he accepts that rather than advocate licensing for those models.

Altman knowingly makes this trade-off and says so plainly. He openly concedes that sub-frontier models will cause harm, and he judges that cost worth paying to keep regulatory attention on catastrophic risk at the top.

I agree with @scottnarmstrong , this is becoming increasingly silly.

The technology extracts proofs from the literature without anyone initially understanding much of what has been extracted. The interesting, creative work starts after the data is extracted.

So either you assume the position that as a company you are in the business of extracting raw data of scientific interest, and then you just stop there and let the scientific community figure it out;

Or you are in the business of authorship and dissemination, thus you are interested in the attribution of a piece of scholarly work… then your are essentially in competition for priority with the scientific community.

I think the latter is very bad choice for OpenAI (I am not even sure how they don’t realize that!), but if you pick that route, you have to play by the same rules of everyone else. 

As much as individuals don’t announce “I will write a paper in two months, but please give me credit now”, OpenAI shouldn’t do that.

I think the “producers of raw scientific data” option would be by far the cleaner one, especially if paired with more transparency on what “raw data” you plan to extract in the future.

I wanted to see if it could build something real, not just a landing page. So I had it build a 3D candy factory game in OpenCode, from a few prompts.

What it made: 
→ Six machines, each with its own 3D model: Dispenser, Boiler, Flavor Mixer, Molder, Sparkle Coater, Packer 
→ Belts that carry items through a production chain, with machines that block or starve when inputs are missing 
→ An economy with coins, upgrades, and customer orders 
→ Live charts for coins per minute and throughput per machine 
→ A minimap, undo/redo, 1x/2x/5x speed, and save/load 
→ Click-to-place building, auto-connected belts, and a "why is it blocked?" helper

It also fixed its own bugs along the way, like a starting layout where every machine was blocked.

Fast, and it handled a multi-file project with real game logic.

Open weights are live. Go build something.
